title: Will An Aging China Save Less?
text:
Will An Aging China Save Less?

Ernan Cui, Yu Wu

Gavekal Dragonomics | 28 Aug 2026

China’s household savings rate has stayed stubbornly high, around 35% of income, for most of the past decade. This stability is surprising as it comes amid rapid demographic changes, with the total population shrinking and the share of the elderly rising. This demographic transformation is only going to accelerate in the coming decade, as a sharp fall in fertility will mean the population becoming even more dominated by the elderly (see The Birth Dearth Deepens). Will this aging of the population finally force a change in China’s high-savings economic model?There are a couple of ways in which demographic changes have been expected to pull down the household savings rate in China. One is through the composition effects of an aging population. Individuals typically build up savings during their working years and spend them down in retirement; as a result, if there are more retired people, the average savings rate should be lower. Another is through generational turnover that changes the dominant pattern of savings behavior. Chinese people whose lives included dramatic shocks, like the Cultural Revolution and the dismantling of the planned economy, are generally thought to be more cautious and risk-averse than the younger generations who have grown up in a more prosperous and stable China. As these newer generations become the largest part of the workforce, they could also pull down the overall savings rate.
